# Properties and Validation {#sec-properties-validation}

::: {.chapter-abstract}
How a file carries "material: 6061-T6" and "mass: 0.324 kg" — and how it carries its own checksum, so that a receiving system can tell whether the geometry survived the trip.
:::

@sec-product-to-shape introduced `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` as a *property definition* — the shape property of a part — and promised the rest of the family.
The same three-record pattern that attaches a shape attaches anything else, and it is how both user attributes and the standard's built-in validation data travel.

## The property pattern {#sec-properties-validation-pattern}

```{.step source="block.step"}
#420 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION('Material','',#5);
#421 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#420,#422);
#422 = REPRESENTATION('',(#423),#165);
#423 = DESCRIPTIVE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM('Material','6061-T6');
```

*(The examples in this chapter are written to the pattern in the CAx Implementor Forum's recommended practices; the exporter used for the running example does not write properties.)*

- **`PROPERTY_DEFINITION`** names the property and says what it is a property *of*.
  `name` is `'Material'`; `definition` is `#5`, the block's product definition.
  The `definition` attribute is the `characterized_definition` SELECT that `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` inherits, though a shape property is narrowed by a rule to product definitions and occurrences.
A plain `PROPERTY_DEFINITION` may use the whole of it: a `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` (a property of the geometry), a `SHAPE_ASPECT` (a property of one feature), or a `NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE` (a property of one occurrence).
- **`PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION`** binds the property to a representation, exactly as `SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION` binds a shape to one.
- **`REPRESENTATION`** is the container, with a context.
  For text properties the context is irrelevant but required; writers reuse the geometric context.
- **`DESCRIPTIVE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM`** carries a string value: `name` `'Material'`, `description` `'6061-T6'`.

For a numeric property the item is a **`MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM`**, and the unit comes back:

```{.step source="block.step"}
#430 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION('Mass','',#5);
#431 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#430,#432);
#432 = REPRESENTATION('',(#433),#165);
#433 = MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM('Mass',MASS_MEASURE(0.324),#434);
#434 = ( MASS_UNIT() NAMED_UNIT(*) SI_UNIT(.KILO.,.GRAM.) );
```

`MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM` is a complex-instance-free way of saying "a representation item that is a measure with unit": a name, a wrapped value, a unit.
The kilogram is `SI_UNIT(.KILO.,.GRAM.)` — the SI base name is `gram`, and the kilogram takes a prefix.
The CAx-IF practice adds two more records to every user attribute: a `GENERAL_PROPERTY` carrying the attribute's name, and a `GENERAL_PROPERTY_ASSOCIATION` tying it to the `PROPERTY_DEFINITION`.
It is the presence of that `GENERAL_PROPERTY` that tells a reader this is a user attribute rather than a validation property.
It is not an AP242 addition: AP203 second edition and AP214 have it too.

This is the mechanism by which a CAD system's custom properties — part number, material, finish, supplier, cost centre — reach a STEP file, when the exporter is configured to send them.
Most are not by default.
When they are, expect one `PROPERTY_DEFINITION` per attribute per product, each with its own representation, and expect the `name` strings to be whatever the CAD system calls the attribute.

## Validation properties {#sec-properties-validation-validation}

The most important use of the property pattern is one the standard's implementors invented and later formalised: **geometric validation properties**.
The writer computes a few numbers that summarise the geometry — volume, surface area, centroid — and puts them in the file.
The reader, after importing, computes the same numbers from what it built and compares.
If they match to within tolerance, the geometry survived; if the volume is off by a face's worth, a face was lost; if the centroid moved, a component is misplaced.

```{.step source="block.step"}
#400 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION('geometric validation property',
  'volume of part',#4);
#401 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#400,#402);
#402 = REPRESENTATION('volume',(#403),#165);
#403 = MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM('volume measure',
  VOLUME_MEASURE(12000.),#404);
#404 = DERIVED_UNIT((#405));
#405 = DERIVED_UNIT_ELEMENT(#166,3.);

#406 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION('geometric validation property',
  'surface area of part',#4);
#407 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#406,#408);
#408 = REPRESENTATION('surface area',(#409),#165);
#409 = MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM('surface area measure',
  AREA_MEASURE(4000.),#410);
#410 = DERIVED_UNIT((#411));
#411 = DERIVED_UNIT_ELEMENT(#166,2.);

#412 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION('geometric validation property',
  'centroid of part',#4);
#413 = PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#412,#414);
#414 = REPRESENTATION('centroid',(#415),#165);
#415 = CARTESIAN_POINT('centre point',(30.,10.,5.));
```

The block: $60 \times 20 \times 10 = 12\,000$ mm$^3$; $2 \times (1200 + 600 + 200) = 4000$ mm$^2$; centre at (30, 10, 5).
Three things make these records findable by a reader that knows nothing else about the file:

- `PROPERTY_DEFINITION.name` is the fixed string `'geometric validation property'`.
- `REPRESENTATION.name` is `'volume'`, `'surface area'` or `'centroid'`.
- The item's name is `'volume measure'`, `'surface area measure'` or `'centre point'`.

Those strings are prescribed by the recommended practice, not by the schema, and every major exporter follows them.
The `definition` points at the `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` (`#4`) — these are properties of the *shape* — and the units are derived: cubic millimetres for volume, square millimetres for area, built from the length unit as @sec-contexts-units described.
The centroid is an ordinary `CARTESIAN_POINT` in the geometric context, so it is in millimetres automatically.

Validation properties extend well beyond solids, as separate families rather than as extensions of this one.
`'assembly validation property'` with `'number of children'` (an `INTEGER_REPRESENTATION_ITEM` in AP242, a `COUNT_MEASURE` in AP214) records how many components an assembly should have, and `'notional solids centroid'` checks that placements composed correctly.
The same pattern with a different `PROPERTY_DEFINITION` name gives `'tessellated validation property'`, `'attribute validation property'`, `'composite validation property'` and `'pmi validation property'`, the last with items named `'number of annotations'`, `'number of views'` and `'affected area'`, so that a receiver can confirm that not just the shape but the annotations arrived.

::: {.callout-note title="Engineering background: Why an exchange format needs a checksum"}
Every step of a geometry exchange can lose information silently.
A face whose surface the importer cannot rebuild is dropped; a solid whose shell no longer closes is quietly converted to a surface body; a component whose placement was read with the frames reversed lands in the wrong place; an inch file read as millimetres is 25.4 times too small.
None of these produce an error.
The file is valid, the import succeeds, and the model is wrong.

Validation properties are the industry's answer.
They are cheap to compute, they are sensitive to exactly the failures that matter — a missing face changes the area; a lost solid changes the volume; a misplaced component changes the centroid; a unit error changes everything — and they are independent of the representation, so a B-rep in one system and a B-rep in another can be compared without either understanding the other's kernel.
Most CAD importers check them automatically and report a discrepancy as a warning.
They are also, for anyone writing tools that transform STEP files, the easiest correctness test there is.
:::

## Where names hide {#sec-properties-validation-names}

The chapter on identity said the part's name is in `PRODUCT.name`.
That is the *product's* name.
Other names in a file:

- **Occurrence names** — `'pin-1'`, `'pin-2'` — are in `NEXT_ASSEMBLY_USAGE_OCCURRENCE.name`.
- **Body names**, in multi-body parts, are in `MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP.name` when the exporter writes them, and in `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION.name` for some others.
- **Face names**, rarely, in `ADVANCED_FACE.name`.
- **Feature names** do not exist.
  A STEP file has no features.
- **Descriptions** of anything are in the entity's `description` attribute, which is `''` or `$` nearly everywhere.
- **File-level metadata** — author, organisation, originating system — is in the header and nowhere else.

A reader that wants "the name of this thing" has to know which thing and look in the right slot; there is no universal name table.

## What is not here {#sec-properties-validation-not-here}

Properties are strings and numbers hung on the product graph.
They are not *parametric*: a mass property does not update when the geometry changes, and a material property does not tell a kernel what density to use unless the reader chooses to interpret it.
They are not *behavioural*: no constraints, no formulas, no design intent.
STEP has parts for some of that — Part 108 for parameterisation and constraints, AP209 for analysis — and almost no CAD exporter writes them.
What travels is the evaluated model and a set of labels on it.

::: {.callout-important title="In brief"}
A property is `PROPERTY_DEFINITION` (name, and what it is a property of) → `PROPERTY_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION` → `REPRESENTATION` → an item: `DESCRIPTIVE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM` for text, `MEASURE_REPRESENTATION_ITEM` with a wrapped value and a unit for numbers.
Validation properties use this pattern with prescribed names — `'geometric validation property'`, `'volume'`, `'surface area'`, `'centroid'` — to carry a checksum of the geometry that the receiving system recomputes and compares.
:::
